title: Wait-free solvability of graph approximate agreement
formal: For every finite nonempty connected simple undirected graph \(G\) and integer \(n\ge1\), define \(W(G,n)\in\{0,1\}\) to be \(1\) exactly when the \(n\)-process graph agreement task below has a deterministic wait-free solution using only atomic read/write registers, and \(0\) otherwise. Determine this solvability function on its entire domain. The benchmark accepts a real-valued function \(g\) with a Lean-checked proof that \[ \forall G\ \forall n\ge1:\quad |g(G,n)-W(G,n)|\le 1/100.\] A mathematically explicit necessary-and-sufficient characterization can specify \(g\); an algorithm deciding solvability from a graph is not additionally required.

source_formulation.text: However, for many graphs it is unknown whether a wait-free solution for approximate agreement exists using only registers.
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 2

why: The question classifies which discrete relaxations of consensus can be implemented despite arbitrary process delays and crashes with the most basic shared-memory objects. Its full resolution connects the geometry of permitted output values with distributed computability, beyond separate algorithms and impossibility results for particular graph families.
status_note: Resolved in the literature by Rybicki and Verbitsky, arXiv:2606.24666v1 (23 June 2026), Corollary 9, accepted at DISC 2026 according to the official regular-paper list checked 14 September 2026. The source task, model, all-process-count quantifiers, theorem and proof were checked at the cited locations. This is a source-based resolution audit; the imported asynchronous computability theorem and topology background have not been independently formalized in Lean, and no Lean benchmark submission is certified.

progress.text: The source records the incomplete classification and new process-dependent impossibility results for graph agreement with clique validity.
Corollary 9 of the new manuscript characterizes all process counts through the connectivity of the clique complex, including the all-process-count contractibility criterion.
The exact task correspondence, characterization and proof locations were reviewed, and the official DISC 2026 list was checked for acceptance. The historical open card is retired as resolved.

category_assignment.reason: Approximate agreement is a wait-free distributed task, not an optimization approximation ratio.

importance.reason: A general solvability classification for a canonical distributed agreement task, relating graph structure, process count and fault tolerance. This historical importance assessment is independent of the newly located resolution.

sentences: Processes receive vertices of a fixed graph and must decide vertices that form a clique despite arbitrary crashes and delays.
When the input vertices already form a clique, every output must be among those input vertices.
The original question asks which graphs and process counts admit deterministic wait-free solutions using only read/write registers.
The accepted 2026 work of Rybicki and Verbitsky characterizes solvability through the connectivity of the graph’s clique complex.
The historical question is therefore retired as resolved in the literature, with its complete statement and provenance preserved.

definitions:
The graph is fixed and known to all processes. Its vertices may be named \(\{0,\ldots,m-1\}\) and its edges given by a symmetric zero-diagonal Boolean matrix; the vertex names have no role in the agreement condition. Processes have distinct identifiers \(1,\ldots,n\). Process \(i\) initially knows its own input vertex \(x_i\in V(G)\), its identifier, \(G\), and \(n\), but no other process’s input. Every vector in \(V(G)^n\) is allowed. A process may irrevocably decide one output vertex \(y_i\). It may crash by ceasing to take steps at any time, including before revealing its input or after deciding.

The communication model is asynchronous shared memory with a countable collection of single-writer, multiple-reader registers, initially containing a distinguished empty value. Registers hold finite binary strings. Each register has a fixed writer; any process can read it. A shared-memory step is one atomic read of one register or one atomic write by its owner. A read returns the most recent written value, or the initial value if there was no write. Processes otherwise perform deterministic local Turing computations using finite descriptions and unrestricted finite storage. Only reads and writes are supplied as communication primitives; there is no clock, failure detector, randomness, oracle, or other atomic object. Each local step and each string written is finite.

An execution is any finite or infinite interleaving of process steps consistent with their programs. Let \(X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\), including inputs of processes that later crash. At each finite prefix let \(Y\) be the set of values already decided. Safety requires that distinct elements of \(Y\) are adjacent in \(G\). It also requires clique validity: if distinct elements of \(X\) are pairwise adjacent, then \(Y\subseteq X\). A singleton is a clique. For non-clique input sets, this validity condition imposes no restriction beyond membership in \(V(G)\). Outputs already decided by a subsequently crashed process still count.

Wait-freedom means that any process that continues taking steps must decide after finitely many of its own steps, regardless of the speeds or permanent stopping of the others; up to \(n-1\) other processes may crash. A protocol for a fixed pair \((G,n)\) consists of finite deterministic programs for the processes. Their sizes, running times and memory are not bounded by a complexity target. The programs may depend on \(G,n\), but not on the full input vector or schedule. Existence is asserted separately for each pair, without requiring a computable synthesis procedure over all graphs.
answer_criterion: Specify a function \(g\) on all finite connected simple graphs and all positive process counts, and give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed absolute \(1/100\) error bound. An exact solvability characterization qualifies; the supplied function need not be integer-valued or computable. Merely repeating the definition as protocol existence does not determine the answer. Both existence and impossibility cases must be justified in the same deterministic read/write model with clique validity. Results for a stronger path-based validity condition or for a fixed graph family do not determine the whole function.

context_blocks.text: The 2022 source uses clique validity: when the inputs already form a clique, processes must choose among those inputs. This is weaker than requiring each output to lie on an induced or shortest path between inputs. The recovered target retains the source’s weaker condition and makes the process count an explicit parameter.

Earlier positive cases included trees, while cycles of length at least four were impossible with at least three processes. Liu enlarged the impossible graph families and proved that the octahedron requires at least four processes for its impossibility result. Thus the number of processes cannot be silently omitted from a classification.

Rybicki and Verbitsky’s Corollary 9 gives the full characterization: \(W(G,n)=1\) exactly when the clique complex of \(G\) is \((n-2)\)-connected. The clique complex consists of all nonempty cliques; its geometric realization is the union of their simplices in Euclidean space. For \(k\ge0\), \(k\)-connected means path-connected with trivial homotopy groups in dimensions \(1,\ldots,k\); equivalently every continuous map from a sphere of one of these dimensions extends to the corresponding ball. The \((-1)\)-connected condition is automatic for the nonempty complexes here. In particular, solvability for every process count is equivalent to contractibility, meaning that the identity map continuously deforms to a constant map.

The June 2026 manuscript’s input and validity definitions match the original question. Its theorem and proof, including the reduction to the standard asynchronous computability theorem, were checked at the cited locations. The official DISC 2026 regular-paper list confirms acceptance. This record is retired because the mathematical classification has appeared; it does not record a submitted or checked Lean benchmark solution.
